演奏鈴鼓可手持鼓框，也可固定在支架或夾鉗上。基本發聲方式包括搖動金屬片、以手或鼓: You can play the tambourine holding the frame in one hand, or fix it to a stand or clamp. The basic ways of sounding it are to shake the jingles, to strike the head and frame with the hand or a stick, or to beat the body against the thigh or hip. Begin with the frame in one hand and the other hand striking the head or frame, then practise swinging the wrist back and forth so that the jingles strike one another in a continuous roll. The advanced thumb roll rubs the thumb, index or middle finger over the head about a centimetre in from the rim, so that the finger bounces quickly; a little wax or a damp fingertip gives more friction, and moving in a figure of 8 keeps the roll going.

鈴鼓具有明亮而清脆的音色，帶有獨特的金屬質感。其音域相對較高，能夠穿透樂隊的整體: The tambourine has a bright, crisp timbre with a distinctive metallic quality. Its range is relatively high, and it carries through the sound of a whole band. When it is struck, the animal skin gives a warm base to the drum sound while the inset metal jingles add a glittering high-frequency ring; the two blend into a timbre rich in layers. Its way of resonating is distinctive: it has the membrane sound of a traditional drum and, because the jingles collide, the brightness of a metal instrument. Next to a plain snare drum the tambourine sounds more lively and joyful; next to the monotony of a triangle it has more warmth and body. These mixed qualities let it both give rhythmic support in an orchestra and, on its own, make a light, catching sound effect.
鈴鼓可見於常規打擊樂組，也可架在鼓組上以鼓棒演奏，或手持敲擊、搖動。它出現在阿爾: The tambourine appears in the standard percussion section; it can also be mounted on a drum kit and played with sticks, or held in the hand and struck or shaken. It is found in the folk music of Albania, the Arab world, the Balkans, Israel, Turkey, Greece, Italy, France and Spain, and in Persian music, samba, gospel, pop, country, rock and classical music. Classical works include Dvořák's Carnival Overture, Bizet's Carmen Suite, Tchaikovsky's Capriccio Italien, The Nutcracker Suite and the fourth movement of the Manfred Symphony, Mahler's Third Symphony, and Good News from Beijing Reaches the Border Villages.
鈴鼓的鼓框多為圓形，來源記載常見木或塑膠，另有資料記木或金屬。發聲部件包括鑲於框: The frame of the tambourine is usually circular; the sources record wood or plastic as common, and other sources say wood or metal. The sounding parts are the metal jingles set into the frame and, in some types, a drumhead made mainly of animal skin, such as sheepskin or calfskin. Those without a head sound from the jingles striking one another. The sources do not record the materials of the clamps, stands, fixings or other fittings, nor the exact alloy of all the frames and jingles.
鈴鼓起源不明，歷史文獻最早見於公元前1700年，先用於古埃及、古代近東，後傳至希: The origin of the tambourine is unknown; it first appears in historical writings in 1700 BC, was used first in ancient Egypt and the ancient Near East, and later reached Greece and elsewhere, coming into Europe by way of merchants or musicians. The Hebrews mostly used it on religious occasions. Its name comes from the French name of a long, narrow Provençal drum, and was influenced by the Arabic name for a drum. In the late 18th century it became popular in England, where composers of salon music wrote as many as 30 different strokes for it; in the late 19th century the Salvation Army made it one of its important rhythm instruments. In the 20th century, with the development of African-American spirituals, gospel music and pop, the headless tambourine came into common use and it became a hand-held percussion instrument.

Its common form is a circular frame of wood, metal or plastic set with several groups of metal jingles; traditionally it has a drumhead of sheepskin or calfskin, and headless variants also exist. It can be held in the hand and struck or shaken, or fixed to a stand or clamp and struck with sticks; for fast rhythms it can be held between the hand and the thigh. Singers, drummers and folk musicians often play it in the folk music of Albania.
